quiz1: Analysis investigates the problem and the requirements: what stakeholders need, how a system will be used, and which domain concepts matter. Design develops a conceptual solution that meets those requirements, including software objects, their collaborations and other structures such as a database schema. Analysis therefore clarifies what should be achieved, while design explains how an appropriate solution will be organized. Implementation turns that design into executable software.

The Unified Modeling Language (UML) is a standardized visual notation used to specify, construct and document system artifacts, particularly in object-oriented software development. Its diagrams describe different views, such as class structure and interactions between objects. UML is a modeling language rather than a development process: knowing its notation does not by itself provide the analysis or design judgment needed to produce a good system.

Iterative development organizes work into short, fixed-length cycles. Each iteration includes analysis, design, implementation and testing, and produces an integrated, tested, executable part of the system. Later iterations enlarge and refine that system. It is evolutionary because requirements, plans and design are revised using feedback from working software, tests and stakeholders. Consequently, the whole specification does not have to be completed before development begins.

The textbook recommends iterations of approximately two to six weeks. This keeps work small enough to manage and provides frequent opportunities for feedback and adaptation. A very short iteration may not produce enough meaningful work for useful evaluation, whereas a long one increases complexity, postpones feedback and allows risks to remain hidden. Iterations should be timeboxed: if the agreed work cannot be completed, reduce the iteration scope and defer lower-priority tasks instead of extending its end date.

Complex software projects involve uncertainty and changing needs, so early specifications and estimates are unlikely to remain completely correct. Feedback from working software and client demonstrations improves requirements; tests and implementation experience improve the design; actual progress improves schedules and estimates; and client or market feedback helps reprioritize features. Adaptation uses this evidence to change the next development step. Repeated build, feedback and adjustment cycles reduce the cost of pursuing incorrect assumptions and help the product converge on stakeholder needs.

Agile Modeling uses lightweight models primarily to improve understanding and communication. Developers sketch the difficult or uncertain parts of a problem or design, rather than attempting to model every detail before programming. Typical practices include simple tools, brief collaborative sessions, evolving several complementary models together and using only enough notation to communicate clearly. Models guide development but are expected to change or be discarded as coding and testing reveal a better design.

A domain model is a visual representation of important conceptual classes or real-world objects in a problem domain, together with relevant attributes and associations. In the textbook's analysis perspective, it does not describe software classes, method implementations or database tables. It provides a shared visual vocabulary that helps people understand the domain and communicate accurately. Its concepts can inspire the names and information in later software classes, reducing the gap between the software representation and the way people understand the business.

Logical architecture is the large-scale organization of software classes into packages, subsystems and layers. It describes the organization of software responsibilities without deciding how the parts will be deployed across processes or physical computers. A layer is a broad, cohesive grouping with responsibility for a major concern, such as user interaction, application and domain logic, or technical services. Higher layers normally request services from lower layers. Strict layering allows calls only to the immediately lower layer, while relaxed layering permits calls across several lower layers.

The essential idea is to divide the software into layers with distinct, cohesive responsibilities and a clear separation of concerns. Lower layers provide more general services, while higher layers are more application-specific. Dependencies should mainly point downward, avoiding direct dependence of lower layers on higher ones. Benefits include reduced coupling and change propagation, greater cohesion and clarity, encapsulated complexity, better reuse of lower-level services, and the possibility of replacing or distributing some layers. Clear boundaries also help developers organize and divide their work.

Model-View Separation keeps domain and application logic independent of a particular user interface. Non-UI objects should not directly reference or manipulate concrete windows or web pages. Conversely, UI objects should handle input, output and UI events, then delegate business operations to non-UI objects rather than performing business calculations themselves. This supports reuse, separate development, alternative or simultaneous views, and testing or execution without the UI. An indirect notification through a general observer interface can preserve the separation because the model need not know the receiver is a view.

Static modeling describes the structure and definitions of a design: packages, classes, attributes, associations and method signatures. UML class diagrams are a typical example; they do not show the detailed logic inside method bodies. Dynamic modeling describes behavior and collaborations: which objects send messages, in what order, and how their methods cooperate to carry out a task. Sequence and communication diagrams are examples. The two views should evolve together, since an interaction may reveal a required method or relationship that must also appear in the static design.

Sequence diagrams make the ordering of messages easy to follow from top to bottom. They offer richer notation and generally stronger tool support, which makes them useful for detailed documentation and reverse-engineered call flows. Their weakness is horizontal expansion: adding participants uses more space to the right. Communication diagrams place objects freely in a two-dimensional network, so they use space efficiently and are easier to rearrange during sketching. However, readers must follow message numbers to determine the sequence, and the notation provides fewer detailed options. The choice depends on the purpose and available space.

Test-Driven Development writes a small executable test before the corresponding production code, then implements enough code to pass and repeats. This encourages tests to be written consistently instead of being postponed or omitted. Writing the test first clarifies the required public interface and behavior. The growing test suite provides repeatable automated verification and quick feedback about regressions. This increases confidence when changing or refactoring code. The immediate challenge of making a test pass can also make testing more satisfying and sustainable for developers.

Creator is a GRASP responsibility-assignment pattern for deciding which class should create an instance of another class. Give class B responsibility for creating an instance of class A when B contains or aggregates A, records A, closely uses A, or has the initialization information needed by A. If several candidates qualify, a containing or aggregating class is usually preferred. For example, a Sale can create its SalesLineItem objects because it contains them. This tends to preserve low coupling because the creator already needs a relationship with the created object.

The Factory pattern described in the textbook assigns object creation to a dedicated helper object, a Pure Fabrication whose responsibility is to construct other objects. It is also called Simple Factory or Concrete Factory; the book notes that it is not itself a GoF pattern and is related to Abstract Factory. Use it when creation is complex, when choosing an implementation should be hidden from clients, or when creation duties would reduce a domain object's cohesion. A factory can also centralize caching or recycling. For example, a services factory can choose and create the appropriate adapter for an external tax service.
quiz2: Object-oriented analysis identifies and describes important concepts and objects in the problem domain, such as Sale, Product and Payment in a retail system. It develops understanding of the domain rather than committing to software classes. Object-oriented design defines software objects, their information, responsibilities and collaborations so that they satisfy the requirements. A design class may therefore include attributes and methods that do not belong in a conceptual domain model. Object-oriented programming then implements those design objects in a language such as Java.

UML as sketch uses informal, incomplete diagrams to explore and communicate selected difficult aspects of a problem or solution. UML as blueprint uses more detailed diagrams to understand existing code through reverse engineering or to guide code generation through forward engineering. UML as programming language aims at a complete executable specification from which code is generated automatically, with development carried out in the UML representation. The textbook favors sketching for agile modeling and distinguishes these three uses from the separate conceptual, specification and implementation perspectives.

Iterative development provides early visible progress through tested working increments. It exposes technical, requirements and usability risks sooner, allowing them to be reduced before they become expensive. Frequent stakeholder feedback and involvement help the evolving system meet real needs. Smaller increments make complexity manageable and reduce prolonged analysis without implementation. Lessons from one iteration can improve the development process in the next. The textbook also reports research associating iterative and evolutionary methods with lower project failure and defect rates and improved productivity.

Waterfall commonly assumes that requirements, designs and plans can be specified accurately near the beginning and then remain relatively stable. The textbook argues that software development usually involves substantial uncertainty and change, so this assumption often fails. Long analysis and design phases based mainly on prediction delay feedback from programming, testing and actual users. Incorrect assumptions can therefore persist until late, when revision is more costly. Iterative development addresses this problem by building and evaluating partial solutions and adapting requirements, designs and plans as evidence becomes available.

Begin with timeboxed requirements work that identifies the main use cases, features and important quality requirements at a high level. Select a small subset that combines architectural significance, business value and risk, and analyze that subset in detail. Plan a fixed-length iteration and break the selected scenarios into tasks. Do enough modeling to guide the difficult design decisions, then implement, test and integrate a working increment. Demonstrate it and collect feedback. Refine requirements and choose the next subset adaptively. Repeat this cycle, allowing detailed understanding and more reliable estimates to emerge instead of attempting complete analysis and design in advance.

First establish the boundary of the system being studied. Next identify the primary actors whose goals are supported by that system, and discover the valuable results each actor wants. Define use cases that satisfy those goals and usually name each one with a verb phrase matching the goal, such as Process Sale. An actor-goal list helps organize the results, while external-event analysis and questions about administration, monitoring and other systems can reveal missed actors or goals. The list evolves iteratively. Related CRUD goals can be grouped into a Manage X use case rather than always creating a separate use case for each small action.

The textbook gives three complementary strategies: reuse or adapt an existing model, consult a conceptual-class category list, and identify nouns or noun phrases in descriptions such as use cases. Useful categories include transactions, transaction line items, products or services, roles, places, events, descriptions and containers. Treat the results as candidates, not as an automatic noun-to-class conversion, because natural language is ambiguous. Review candidates against the current domain and iteration scope, use the domain's own vocabulary, and distinguish meaningful concepts from simple attributes and software implementation artifacts.

Description classes are useful when information about a kind of item or service must exist independently of particular examples. They prevent important information from disappearing when the last instance is removed and reduce duplication of shared descriptive data. For example, ProductDescription can hold an item's name, identifier and standard price, while individual Item instances represent physical goods. If all goods are sold, the description still remains. The same reasoning applies to services, such as keeping a FlightDescription even when no particular flight is scheduled.

A System Sequence Diagram (SSD) shows one scenario of a use case in terms of external actors, the events they send to a system, the order of those events and relevant responses or interactions with other systems. It treats each system as a black box and concentrates on events crossing the boundary, rather than internal software objects. Drawing an SSD makes externally visible behavior and required system operations explicit before detailed object design. These operations provide input to operation contracts and to the interaction diagrams that later explain how collaborating software objects realize the behavior.

Software architecture concerns the significant, large-scale decisions about a system. These include its major structural elements and interfaces, their responsibilities and collaborations, how they are composed into larger subsystems, and the architectural style guiding that organization. It also reflects the important motivations and constraints behind those decisions. Logical architecture addresses the organization of software elements, whereas deployment architecture concerns their placement in processes and computers. Architecture therefore includes both structure and important behavior, rather than being only a diagram of modules.

A design pattern is a named description of a recurring design problem and a reusable solution approach that can be applied in different contexts. A useful pattern explains when the solution applies, the forces and trade-offs involved, and relevant variations or implementation issues. Patterns capture established design experience rather than claiming every solution is a new invention. Their shared names make complex ideas easier to remember and communicate, help developers reason about responsibility assignment, and provide guidance when evaluating design alternatives. They are adaptable guidance, not a substitute for judgment about the actual problem.

Attribute visibility exists when A keeps a reference to B in one of its attributes; it usually lasts with the relationship between the objects. Parameter visibility exists when B is passed to a method of A and is available within that call. Local visibility exists when a method of A creates or obtains B and uses it through a local reference. Global visibility exists when B is available through a globally accessible reference or access mechanism. The purpose is to ensure that B is visible to A whenever A must send B a message; visibility is not merely a list of public and private access modifiers.

Information Expert is the GRASP principle of assigning a responsibility to the class that has the information necessary to fulfill it. The relevant information may be the object's own state, its related objects or values it can derive. For example, a Sale knows its line items and can calculate their combined total, while each SalesLineItem can calculate its subtotal using its quantity and associated price information. Several partial experts may collaborate when the required information is distributed. The principle should be evaluated alongside low coupling and high cohesion, rather than used to mix unrelated technical duties into a domain object.

In GRASP, a controller is the first non-UI object that receives and coordinates a system-operation request from the UI. It may represent the overall system, a device or subsystem, or a particular use case or session. Its basic role is to delegate work to suitable collaborating objects and, where necessary, coordinate the state or permitted sequence of a use case. It should not perform all business work itself or become a bloated class. This differs from a web MVC controller, which mainly manages input and page flow in the presentation layer and can delegate to an application-level controller or service.

Adapter resolves incompatible interfaces by introducing an intermediate object that translates a component's original interface into the interface expected by its client. Use it when existing or third-party components cannot be changed, or when several similar external services offer different APIs but the application needs a stable internal interface. In the textbook's POS example, separate adapters translate requests for tax calculation or accounting into the protocols expected by different external providers. Clients depend on the consistent internal interface, which helps protect them from variations in the external components.
